strTooltip: [them-firstname] may have advice for how to prove your loyalty to Titan.
strDesc:
You approach Pan Tao at his usual smoking spot and ask him how someone like you can prove your loyalty to the Titan cause.  

"Few options," Tao says. "First is territory. The whole belt is in a kind of King of the Hill situation. If you trade for a Titan beacon, you can take it out to unclaimed space near some profitable asteroids. Deploy it and we have eyes on those rocks. Keeps our supply lines open."

"Xinhua likes to throw out their own beacons, so you could always blow those up. That's kinda fun, and the brass gets a big kick out of it."

"If you're feeling froggy, you could always jump. By that I mean: sieze or destroy a Xinhua allied vessel. Demand their surrender or, ya know. Boom."

"Lastly, you can hit the mines. Plenty of good rocks left. Get some ore and sell it to one of our faction kiosks here. That gets you good scrip, plus attaboys from the right folks. 

"Besides that, you could try and run special missions for Mr. Wayne. He doesn't give them to everybody, so if he trusts you to handle it, it's probably a good bet. Check the planter up near 'The Mouth' for messages."

Pan Tao is physically slight for a dock worker. You find him leaning against a wall, lit cigarette in a hand beating a staccato pattern against the rock face.

"Pan Tao," you say, not quite a question.

"Shoot," he says, not quite paying attention.

"How do you know Benjamin Choong?"

Pan squints in your direction, taking a drag from the cig. "Drinking buddy of mine. Why, what's he done?"

"Nothing for quite some time," you say. "He's missing. Some buddy you are."

"Hey pal," he says, "fuck you. I don't know you. Why don't you make like Ben Choong and get lost." He goes back to watching the cargo drones scooting up and down the bore. 

You snap your fingers in his face. "Cut the shit. Whoever turned his place over didn't catch the handwritten sheet of paper with your name on it. Was it you, dumbass?"

That gets his attention. "You're serious," he says. You are. He groans. "That fucking moron ... I don't get paid enough to deal with this shit." He shakes his head. "There's a bar in downtown Calico. Angel Wings. Go there. You'll find the guy you want to talk to. Now leave me alone," he says tiredly, "this was supposed to be my break."
strTooltip: 'Pan Tao' ... that was one of the names on the note in Choong's apartment.

strDesc: [us] gives [them] a startled look and says to follow them to somewhere more private and await further contact.

You arrive at Angel Wings in seventeen minutes. There's one man at the bar. It's a big hat he's wearing, a white Stetson homage, to go with the blue flannel shirt and jeans. He pumps your hand and the shirt cuff brushes your fingers - perfectly smooth. There's no way it's real flannel. "John Wayne, at your service, sir." He holds up two fingers. Two shot glasses full to the brim slide down the bar, not spilling a drop. He's tall and gaunt, almost cadaverous. Brown skin which could be a tan job or some melanin in his family tree. He downs his shot and waits for you expectantly. It burns your throat. He nods slowly. "If you can hold your liquor we'll have no trouble." He's already holding up a hand for two more. "Now listen to me," he says, his hand held up, before you can get a word in edgewise. "We're going to do shots here until we can't see straight. Then we'll go down the street to Palmers. A few more there. Then upspin to The Red Door. Two there, and then I'm gonna get in a fight. You watch my back. Xinhua sailors are loaded with scrip, we take it, it's ours. We hit the Aphrodite. I'm on a hot streak, I won 5 grand this week. We go big, yeah? Follow my lead. After that, I know a guy, Muhammad or Mustafa or something. He knows guys, girls, whatever you like. We put all that together," he says, taking his delivered shot, "and our night is set." You leave your glass where it is for now. "Did you kill Benjamin Choong?" He grimaces. "I dunno, maybe. What's he look like?" "If you don't know, you're wasting my time." "Alright, alright," he says, waving a hand. "Settle down. Cool customer, you. No, I di'nt kill him. He went missing on Ceres. All kinds'a people do." He pulls up his shirt to show the ivory white revolver at his hip. "I'm carrying. You should be too." "You're not even trying to hide what you are. Why?" You look him up and down, the ridiculous caricature of a man. "You stick out like a sore thumb." He considers you at length. It's a surprisingly canny gaze from someone consuming that much liquor. "Well, son," he says slowly, "this is a war. You best know that by now. And war has rules." He sees your expression. "Oh, sure, folks break 'em. But they're there. Least for a little while. And hell, I'm alive, ain't I?" He grins. "'He clasps the crag with crooked hands, close to the sun in lonely lands, ring'd with the azure world, he stands.'" "What was that?" His face darkens. "That's poetry, fucknuts. Now," he steadies his gaze on you. "In the words of the late great Mr. Seger - Pete, not Bob mind you. I hate that Night Moves shit - Which side are you on?"

Isambard's instructions take you to Benjamin Choong's apartment without much difficulty. The residence is a small econo flat nestled among dozens of others in a relatively high rent area of the station. The line of identical doors gives you no reason to pause but Choong's, near the end, is the only one flashing with a green indicator. Clearly, it is unlocked. You step inside.

The place has been ransacked. What clearly began as a tidy living and work space now shows signs of intense struggle. Every bin and rack in the flat gapes open like a yawning mouth. The floor is covered with the guts of terminals: power sources and leads and motherboards. No drives in near sight. Whoever came here knew what they were looking for.

Choong is nowhere to be found.

Perhaps something here will give you insight into what happened. Where do you look first?
strTooltip: The door panel reads Benjamin Choong

strDesc: The bed is high quality, expensive, but unmade. You wonder if Choong was here when he was spirited away in such a hurry. Must have been a rude awakening.

Of all the spaces in your vision, the workbench is the most ruined. Stripped terminals, shattered labware, and tangles of electronics cover the surface. In the center of the table, a clear lack of debris. Even the light layer of dust around the rest of the apartment does not reach here.

Below the vacancy you find a matchbook. It is from a bar here on Port Mojave. Inside, a note written in faint ink. A contact number, and initials below it: PT.
You see a half open fridge, a small dining table with a single chair, and various kitchen items clearly thrown to the ground during the haphazard search.

It remains relatively untouched. Expensive high nutrient foodstuffs are aligned in neat rows. You see about a dozen water bottles, all full, along with a batch of refrigerated supplements, some of which you do not recognize. Choong clearly knew how to take care of himself. Why do you find yourself thinking of him in the past tense?
You find an empty coffee cup, a handheld terminal smashed beyond repair and stripped of its drive, and a paperback book. Not cheap, those. Something called The Day of the Triffids by John Wyndham.

Broken dishware, shattered glass, and assorted papers litter the ground here. You rummage through the papers but they present in a language so erudite as to be illegible to you. Mentions of rare mineral compounds standout, as well as their properties when combusted at certain temperatures. Just as you are about to give up here you glimpse a splash of vibrant color in the wastebasket. You take a closer look. A bouquet of flowers? You retrieve the arrangement. You lean down to smell them but find no odor. They feel fragile, cold, crosshatched. Paper, then. An impressive feat, creating all these by hand. Inside, there is a note: Thank you for meeting with me. No need to look me up next time you are on The Ring. I will find you. - Francisco Ortega
About a dozen containers of various sizes line the walls. Some are embedded in the floor. Where to start?
Nothing here but a collection of research tomes. You are impressed by the range of disciplines covered: mathematics, engineering, art, chemistry, and the histories of ancient Earth civilizations.
This set, near the workbench, is full of tools and small parts. Some remain neatly organized. Others are knocked to the ground.
These appear meant for large item storage. Rolls of textile, stacks of thin metal sheeting, measured glassware, some larger tools and ... something behind the soldering iron there? A seam?

You move the tools aside and press the seam softly. It releases a spring and pops open a tiny hatch, not much larger than the palm of your hand. Inside you find a tiny black notebook. It is a graphed ledger penned in a neat hand. Names, dates, and a final column, unlabeled at the top, but with entries behind each name. John Wayne (GalCon) Francisco Ortega (Xinhua) Han Xiaoli (GalCon Double) Lawrence Masterson (GalCon) Pan Tao (GalCon) Flipping to the very back page of the notebook, you find two additional lines cw GalGon: Q: Where is true West? A: Follow the evening redness. cw Xinhua: Q: Have you ever grown nightshades? A: Only in borrowed soil.
strSetPlotObjective: name|Proxy War: Ben's List|ct|TIsProspectorBCRSorBCER|desc|Try to find one of the names from Ben's notebook.

strTooltip: [them-firstname] may have advice for how to prove your loyalty to Xinhua.
strDesc:
You approach Francisco Ortega. He's looking jumpy as usual. Careful as you can, you ask how someone like you can prove your loyalty to the Xinhua cause.  

"You have a few options,"  Ortega starts.

"First is territory. The whole belt is in open conflict. Might makes right. If you trade for a Xinhua beacon, you can take it out to unclaimed space near some profitable asteroids. Deploy it and we have eyes on those rocks. Keeps our supply lines open."

"Titan's deploying their own beacons, you could neutralize them - so long as you feel safe in enemy territory."

"The cause can always use able pilots. If you're feeling brave, you can sieze or destroy a Titan allied vessel. Demand their surrender, or take them out by force."

"Lastly, mining. The belt is rich. If you find some ore, you can sell it to one of our faction kiosks here. That gets you scrip for more weapons and beacons, and it helps fill our coffers."

"Besides that, you could try and run special ... errands for our mutual friend. Check the coffee machine. It's a dead drop, so we don't have to keep meeting like this."

strTooltip: [them-firstname]'s social profile matches a name on Choong's hidden document. Maybe [them-subj] [knows] something.
strDesc:
The man is two bites in to a mushroom burger. "Francisco Ortega?" you ask.

"Yes?" he says, digging in a bag for a sauce capsule.

"I'm looking for Benjaming Choong."

Ortega chokes, coughing up crumbs and a single mushy chunk. He whirls about. "Who the hell are you? What outfit are you from?" he hisses. You fold your arms and give him nothing. He scans the crowd anxiously. "I'll get ahold of someone with clearance. The Fountain, half an hour. Be there."

He shoulders past you, eager to pretend you've never met.

strTooltip: It's a short walk away. You'll be back before you know it.
strDesc:
Exposed water pipes from the recycling plant run over your head, humming and sloshing. You laugh, inaudible to anyone but you, such is the power of the noise. This is the 'Fountain', a very large section of the ring, and the closest thing to a public space on the station. Benches and standing rocks suggest a landscape garden, along with a few odd planters. The benches are full of couples enjoying discrete conversation. Up the curve of the ring, jogging toward you, there's a squad of Coalition marines on first shift PT.

Your roving gaze lands on someone staring at you. Red cheongsam, Afro-Asian. Their hand falls gracefully, palm out. An invitation.

You fall into step beside them. Sandalwood scent, you think, and self-consciously you try to remember the last time you'd had such a luxury for yourself. They have enough makeup on that maybe they don't have any at all. Maybe they just have a lucky complexion.

"-?" you say, your voice lost to the water overhead. "Did you kill Ben Choong?"

They don't look at you as they reply. "I sincerely hope not," they say. Their accent is, of all things, American, complete with vocal fry. "I'm answering for my employer, right. I was in bed forty minutes ago." 

"You hope not?"

"Lower your voice," they say steadily. "Even here. If you get out of hand, I have to get my security involved, or risk my cover." A smile plays at the corner of their mouth. "Understood?"

With a glance over your shoulder, you get the sense that someone of far greater mass than you is keeping a respectful but fixed distance. 

"Understood, sure," you reply, trying to match their tone. "And you understand this: you tell me what's going on or I'm going to act like an unstable space captain who just did 3 AU for nothing."

They stop to admire a particularly interesting rock on a solid white display plinth. You stare at their profile until they nod, acquiescing. Then you look at the rock too.

"We're clear, Captain. And believe me, I would love to tell you what I know. But first, I have to know where you stand. So?"

strTitle: Express Loyalty to GalCon and Titan
strDesc:
"Well hell yeah. Another soldier for the good guys." 

"Now let's see here," Wayne continues. "I can't really tell if you paint houses. Hard to gather sometimes. But if wetwork ain't your bailiwick we could always use a cracker. But I wouldn't recommend that myself. Xinhua runners don't fuck around. Two steps in and suddenly you'll find yourself with a whole lotta not-so-pretty pictures on a data card you'd swear you wiped ages ago. Happened to a buddy of mine a couple years back and he's still suckin air down Prokofiev way. I should send him a package..."

"Hate to hear it, hombre," Wayne says. "I guess this is sayonara."  

He tips his cap and holds up two more fingers. "Shot for the road?"

He drains the little cup like he's done it a million times before. You eye your own drink with naked suspicion, given the circumstances. 

"More for me then, I guess," he says, and drinks your glass down. He unfolds himself off the stool and saunters out of the bar. 

John Wayne, huh? At least the name won't be hard to remember.

Especially since he left you with the tab.

strTitle: Express Ambivalence to The Proxy Powers
strDesc:
"Playing the field, I see," Wayne says. He winks. "I like someone who keeps their options open. More money in that. Although you might get dead."

Wayne holds up another two fingers without asking if you're drinking. 

"Well," he says. "I ain't gonna help you no more because you don't know who you work for and I sure as shit don't neither."

The shots arrive and he downs both before walking out without so much as an adios. 

John Wayne, huh? An odd presence, to say the least.

He left you with the tab.

"That's reassuring, at least," they say. "If not your...aggressive overtures. But loyalty must be proved, you see. So. A test."

"Let's hear it," you reply.

"There's a coffee kiosk on the main floor of BCRS. Not much to it. Check beneath the discarded pouches, though, and you might find what you're looking for."

"And what's that?"

They bend down to inspect the rock more closely. You wonder, briefly, if a stone could hold the answer to all your questions.

"You know, back on Earth," they begin. "Before the ablation cascade took the whole world from us. Some would say our nation thinks not in decades but in centuries."

They turn and look up at you from below. 

"Such patience might serve you well now, Captain," they say before standing, dusting off their hands, and walking back up the pathway the way they came.
strSetPlotObjective: name|Proxy War: Prove Your Loyalty|ct|TIsProspectorBCRS|desc|Prove your worth with Xinhua. Maybe Ortega can help?

strTitle: Express Ambivalence to The Proxy Powers
strDesc:
"Lukewarm," they say. "Never a good sign. You'll end up spat from God's mouth with an attitude like that."

"Never been a fan of blind loyalty," you reply. 

"It's time you saw, then," they say.

And with that, they continue their walk up the path.

strTitle: Express Loyalty to GalCon and Titan
strDesc:
"Ah," they say. "A shame. I had such high hopes for you."

"What is that supposed to mean?" you ask.

"The tides are turning, Captain. You'll find it wise not to be swept up in the undertow," they say.

And with that, they continue their walk up the path.

As you try to work out where you've been deposited, you hear a raspy voice at your shoulder: "Got a light?" A funny little woman waves an unlit Viceroy at you. She has thick white eyebrows, thick black framed glasses, and an accent you cannot place. She doesn't look like the hawkers you narrowly escaped. "Are you going to try to sell me something?" you ask. She gestures with the cigarette. "Probably not." Once the cigarette is lit, she takes a satisfied drag, exhaling a long stream through her nostrils. "You're just off the [us-shipname], correct?" "How did you know that?" "Relax," she says airily. "It's all anyone talks about on the Ring. Every miner here is a fat walking bag of money, and everyone else wants some. Retail surveillance is building your personality profile as we speak. Face, name, how long you'd glance at her tits," she indicates an erotic advertisement you've not yet seen, "how many steps you've taken, where you stopped, where you've come from, where you're going." She gives you a moment to chew on that, then indicates herself. "Eleni Konstantinidis. I'm a trader, like you, of a sort. Us ship captains look out for one another. Let me buy you a coffee."

Despite her stated lack of interest in selling you anything, or perhaps because of it, you're wary. You follow her unerring footsteps just off the concourse to an equally crowded but less rancidly desperate intersection, and into a dimly lit coffee house there.

Low lighting, better acoustics, and the return of your personal space are all immediate and ongoing reliefs. The clientele resemble Eleni in demeanour if not in look: serious men and women sit one-on-one in private booths, engaged in fierce but inaudible debate. The real deals are made here.

Eleni banters briefly in Greek with the host, who seats you at her favourite booth.

"Let's start with the basics of life in Ceres space," she says, "and this will go much quicker if I don't have to guess what you don't know. Like the war. You know about the war?"

"I don't know," you say. "Do I?"

"Exactly," says Eleni. "So ask me about the war. Thank you, Niko." The host puts a fresh pot and two china cups between you. You take a sip, and have to stop yourself from spilling in surprise, without contest, the best coffee you've ever tasted.

Eleni fiddles with her necklace, shifting the pearls along the string with one hand. It's a chintzy fake, in your estimation. Perhaps it has sentimental value. "It's like this. Mars and Titan - Xinhua and the United States. They got all the money. They want, they need, metal. There's metal out there, all over, oodles of it, sitting in the asteroids. In the Belt, Jupiter, doesn't matter. But they got problems. It's an ocean of soup, and they've both got tiny little plastic spoons." She holds up a complimentary tiny plastic spoon wrapped in packaging, and tosses it aside. "Ever tried cracking an asteroid, gathering up all the dust and rock, sifting through it all for the shit that isn't worthless? And then, you've got a fuckload of kamacite and your dick in your hands, but you want a steel coil you can sell. Have you got a blast furnace and water enough to swim in?" She doesn't wait for you to answer. "Fuck that noise. It's expensive, time-consuming, and dangerous. They'd much rather us do it for them." "I'm familiar with mining," you say. "Then you'll be familiar with how mining ships go missing around here," she says flatly, "and by 'go missing', I mean they were last seen entering the torpedo envelope of an unaligned ship before suffering complete existence failure. They're not fucking around, my young friend. There's a killing to be made here." She leans forward, peering over her glasses as they ever so slightly slip down her nose. "Be sure the killing's not made of you." "Nice." "Thank you." She sips her coffee.

strTitle: Ask her who's doing the killing
strDesc:
Eleni dips her finger in the saucer. She draws on the placemat: Ring station, and its parent body Ceres, which both look unhelpfully like messy brown coffee circles. She draws another one, big, with a bunch of dots. 

"That's us, Ring Station and Ceres, and that's them, King Jupiter and his moons. As sure as they're here in secret, blasting us to pieces whenever we're nodding off behind the wheel, our brave boys and girls are over there doing the same to the Galileans."

"The station can't stop the Galileans operating here?"

"The station is trying," she says. "Everyone living in Calico City is sick of the corporate yoke, and they're the Coalition's main source of miners. There's a sliver of overlap in the Venn diagram between those pissed off folks and all the happy-go-lucky sods on the concourse outside, in that Bosch painting," she says. You nod like you've seen the painting before, or for that matter, any painting before. Aren't paintings supposed to be beautiful?

"If they push too hard, the people will push back. And the Coalition will find themselves with another revolution, right here on their front doorstep."

strTitle: Ask why the Galileans care so much
strDesc:
"Bigger picture," you ask, "why's the competition so fierce? Why blow up each other's ships?"

"It's the economy, stupid." You frown. She smiles indulgently, as if to a favoured child. "Look it up sometime, I'm not calling you stupid. All wars are fought for money, or things that turn into money, like power or control or slaves. Ceres and Jupiter are selling all this stuff to Mars and Titan, and whoever secures the Belt can starve their opponent.

"Xinhua controls the Coalition, by complicated financial wizardry. Every corp with a stake, if you dig enough, is partly or wholly owned by someone else, and they're owned by someone else again, et cetera, et cetera, until eventually you get to Xinhua."

"And Titan?"

"Jupiter," she says, "or, the Galilean Confederacy, they're calling it these days. They've got more moons than brain cells. Overthrew the Troy-Jupiter Group, declared for themselves, and now Titan's the only thing propping them up. Your guess is as good as mine whether they make it five years, or five more weeks."

"So I've got it clear," you say slowly, "you're saying that Xinhua and the US are in a cold war to control the Belt, but the prize in controlling the Belt, is that it would help win a war over the Belt?"

She mulls over the sentence, then raises her hand to the host for a refill. "That's pretty much it," she says.

"Suit yourself," she says. Without missing a beat she veers into the nearest brothel.

Time-to-shop, indeed.

In your inbox, you find a message regarding another message: ZaraFone, an odd little outfit that provides a professional, comfortable environment for interplanetary communication, has a video waiting for you, sender withheld. And of course you may not watch it on your device, no; you must go there physically and sit in a booth and commune. How else can they profit?

When you get a few minutes to yourself, you pass by ZaraFone. A clerk shows you to your booth, activates an incense vaporiser, and leaves a hot pouch of green tea slowly spinning in the air by your shoulder. They close the door behind them.

The lights dim. Your pleather chair has a chunky keyboard in one arm, with which you instruct the room to play the message.

Isamard snaps into existence on the screen. She's in a recording booth of her own, but whether that's next door or on another planet is impossible to know. "Hello, young [us-custom-characterGenderCond|man|lady|... person]. It is me: Isambard Cruz! We met not long ago. Did not talk much, but sometimes, is how strong bonds are forged." She has storage bricks piled nearby, all set to travel mode. Her cat is in a pet carrier atop the pile. "And you showed polite interest in Jomari. That counts a lot." She sniffs. "I watched the tape you found. Perhaps I am a hypocrite. Don't care. Not important. The tape, it worries me. Abacho and friends are in danger. With the law and ... with others. Avoid them. Or," she shrugs with a quirk of her mouth, "go see them. Is your funeral." Not the best timing. Would it have killed her to call when you were both on station? ... Did she think it would?

Isambard continues after a moment, developing a cryptic little grin. "I have a clue for you, if you avoid funeral. I recognise a man in the video. The student in the classroom, put camera up his nose. He work for me many years ago. He was older - he is older now too - but is him, I am certain. Benjamin Choong," she says, enunciating clearly, and repeats it for emphasis. "With two o's.

"He lives on Ring Station at Ceres, in the old hub. He won't return my message ... I have address. Take your ship, fly to Ceres, go to his apartment. Maybe he tell you why his private video was on mysterious VHS. And you do wellness check. Leave reply for me with ZaraFone, please."

She reaches without looking and rubs her cat - Jomari? - Jomari's head through the carrier bars. "I would go, but I fear the danger will come for me too. Instead I go where no one will look. Therefore I need itinerant ship detective - and here you are! Too perfect arrangement not to ask."

She smiles ruefully. "Having watched this message, you are plus two hundred thousand US dollars. Use it to get to Ceres - any remainder, you keep. If you take the money but don't go, you are bad person, and will meet a sticky end. All right. Good luck. Good bye now." She hits a button, and the video ends. Not one for ceremony.

You check your account. As promised it's healthier by two hundred grand. And all it cost was the threat of a curse from an old Filipina.

As leads go, it's slim. As incentives go, it's weak. But it's all you've got. If you want to find out who made that tape, it looks like you've got to get your ass to Ceres.
strSetPlotObjective: name|The Videotape: Benjamin Choong|ct|CTPLOT_Ceres_Is_ChoongDoor|desc|Head to Ben Choong's last known address on Old Ring Station, Ceres.

strDesc: You return to a central location in the apartment and look around, deciding where to search next.
strTooltip: The door panel reads Benjamin Choong

strDesc: You return to Choong's apartment, wondering if there's something you might have missed. You look around, wondering where to check first.

strDesc:
You spend some time watching the city at work, from a vantage point at the terminal overlook. You grip a yellow and black striped safety railing for security - it's the only such safety device you can see. The Ceresians seem very comfortable floating themselves from building to building, sailing through unmarked volumes that they somehow know are for public transit, without ever once colliding. A helpful plaque advises that visitors and non-residents use software assistance to travel these arteries.

Before too long, as you follow the luminous floating arrows overlaid in your PDA's viewfinder, you have your first collision. There are two types of traveling Ceresians: single, harried looking salarymen, and gaggles of youths bantering in American drawls. It's the latter that you hit, though you could've sworn you were following your arrow correctly. Somehow a limb gets hooked and then you smack through the middle of them like a bowling ball.

Their voices turn from loud and happy to shrill and angry. A tall boy in a polo shirt emblazoned with a scowling Vegeta disentangles himself from his friends. He floats toward you, stopping gracefully with a blast from his wrist jets. "Hey, Offworld," he says, and it's clearly meant as a disparaging form of address. "You made a mistake just now. You mind apologising to my friends here?"

His right hand crosses to his left hip. A twitch of his fingers pulls his shirt back just enough to reveal the distinctive wooden grip of a Colt 1911 poking out the waistband of his jeans.

"It was totally my fault," you say. "I don't know how to get around yet. I hope nobody was hurt."

"Mm," he says, considering. "That dog ain't gonna hunt." His friends, now reformed as a group of eager spectators, giggle and snicker.

"Someone oughta teach you how to apologise properly, Offworld," he says, gripping the pistol butt in hand. "Someone like me."

"Sure, if you're good at apologising, you can give me some pointers," you say. The laughter from his friends stops. Uh-oh. It turns out their brains are developed enough to detect irony.

He draws the gun. His followers sigh happily. His hand is down for now, but his eyes - his eyes are pinpricks of rage. What the hell is this kid's problem?

"Beg, Offworld," he says. "Beg for your life."

"Please don't kill me," you say fervently. "I really, really, really don't want to die, and not like this, not over some accident." "Not like this?" he repeats, incensed. "It would be an honour to die by my hand. I've sent four souls to Hell. Wish you to join them?" Christ, now he's talking like a Shakespeare villain. "No, no sir," you say smartly. Outside the tunnel vision you've fixed on this psychopathic teen brandishing a museum piece, you can sense the flow of street traffic ignoring the street drama with uncanny propriety. "I wish not to dishonour you by wasting your bullet on worthless offworld trash like myself." He cocks his head. "That wasn't half bad, in truth." One of his lackeys nods sincerely. "Okay. I'll spare your miserable life. But maybe I'll put one arm out of commission, so you don't forget." He takes aim, his gun hand drifting lazily down to target your shoulder.

"CHADWICK O'NEILL," bellows a woman's voice from above. The tall youth - Chadwick - cringes at once, and the gun is no longer pointed at you. You release a breath you didn't know you'd held.

A short older woman - though she couldn't be much past forty - swoops down like an angel. She plants herself in front of Chadwick, who can't meet her look. His friends begin drifting away in ones and twos. "What would your mother say if she saw you mistreating this clumsy foreigner? What about your father, Heaven rest his soul?"

"It wasn't like that, Aunt Liz," Chadwick says to the ground. "I was only -"

Aunt Liz smacks him backhand across the face. It's not for show. She's wearing rings. Blood spirals away toward the city lights. She hits him again exactly as hard. When he raises his head, he already has a bruise. His murderous exterior is shattered, and a frightened child peers through it.

"Go to your room," she says. Quietly said, but somehow the entire street will have heard it. Chadwick backs up as fast as he can, flipping and shooting off on his gas jets without any of his former grace.

Aunt Liz - presumably Liz, to you - drifts over to her second priority. "Thank you," you say. "I don't know what I did, but -"

"Silence, Offworld," she says. There's no venom to it, but it's much more cutting than when her nephew said it. "I am speaking. If you do not have one, buy a gun and carry it openly. Without it you will invite random violence, or unwanted sexual attention."

"Are you serious?" you say.

"Yes," she says. "It would be best for you to handle your business here, and depart from Calico as soon as you are able."

She turns on one heel jet and leaves.

strTitle: Ask about Ceres and Calico City
strDesc:
"Calico City is kind of a crazy place, right?" you say.

"What do you expect? An American colony abandoned by its creditors long ago; then along comes Xinhua." She shrugs. "Isolated, xenophobic, kept in arrested development by a foreign superpower, desperately clutching to their myths of a glorious past - all things considered, and taking the long view, they're quite a normal people. They've been taught to worship a way of life that never was ..." 

She lingers on the thought, then plows on a little more brusquely. "Fucked up is normal, on this world stage of ours." She leans forward and whispers a secret to you. "The hot springs are divine. Cryovolcanic mineral water is very good for the skin."

"I'll have to check those out," you say.

"Mm, well, make sure you're armed at all times. They like their cowboy movies. If you offend someone -" she cocks a finger-pistol at you. "Pew! Pew, pew!" 

Perhaps some people never get the hang of onomatopoeia.

"What's the story with the Galilean Confederacy?"

"Oof, where to begin," she says. "You know about Troy-Jupiter, all that?"

"Kind of," you say.

"You might've seen them in the headlines a few years back. The Troy-Jupiter Group. Local oligarchs of Jupiter; most of it, anyway, twenty moons' worth. A cautionary tale," she wags a finger, "on how much one may starve the serfdom before they do something about it."

"Food was that scarce?" you say doubtfully.

"Of course it wasn't," she says. She smiles. "Not really, anyway. A few shipments went missing that really ought to have made it there. Regardless, who do you think was first on half rations?"

"The executives and their families, as a way of gracefully admitting fault," you say. Eleni snorts. "Probably law enforcement too, to show solidarity."

"The latter actually happened," she says, "and that's how we got the Galilean Confederacy, and why Troy-Jupiter is no more."

"I'm not apologising for anything," you say. "You ran into me. I saw the whole thing - I was there."

He draws the piece. "I have to burn this shirt," he says thoughtfully. "Because it got Offworld sweat on it, or it got Offworld blood on it." He levels it at you. "The choice is yours. Beg, Offworld."

You let your hand drift to your armament, too.

"If I made a mistake, it won't be me who pays for it," you say evenly. "Your friends look like adults." A harmless untruth. "If they're injured, they can speak for themselves."

You lock eyes. It's not hard to get the measure of him. He needs to save face, and if you back down, he can't. He breaks his gaze first. He grins boyishly at his crew, who look none the worse for wear.

"I think we're good here," he says. Suddenly he's friendly, even charming. "Welcome to Calico, friend. We hope you enjoy your visit."

They retreat in good order. Nobody on the street has batted an eyelid.

What the hell is wrong with this place?

"Sure, I can do this," you say. "Do you guys lick boots here? Where do you stand on boots?" A vein pulses in his forehead. "Okay, not that. How about this: I'll make it up to you. Call your mother. I'll take her out to dinner. Treat her right, pay for everything, eat her box, call her in the morning." Damn, whispers one of the posse, in reverence or disgust. You spread your hands. "Well? Where's my bullet, guy? I've got somewhere to be." Tears forming at the corner of his eyes, he lowers the gun. He drifts away, shoulders hunched. One of the girls swoops after him, concerned. Dollars to donuts, that thing was a replica. Or unloaded. You look at his retreating back, annoyed as you are mystified. One of his friends passes you, reproachful look on his face. "Not cool," he says. "Chad's going through a tough time right now." You nod, nonplussed. To reply would be a waste of effort.

strTitle: Ask What In God's Name He Is Talking About
strDesc:
"Moles, fucknuts! Xinhua rats. Place is lousy with 'em. Sometimes we scare 'em up hackin and other times, well. Measures more drastic, if you get my meaning."

"Now here's how you suss 'em out," Wayne leans in so close you can smell the Bismertnaya on his breath. "They train em up good back on Mars. Computer shit, like I said, but fightin' too. Hand to hand, real close quarters. They like to get in and out unseen, so keep an eye out for the sneaky ones. They're cruel little bastards, but they aren't dumb. Most of em are a hell of a lot smarter than me, and that's sayin' something."

"Anyway," he says. "You meet someone like that, more than likely that's our mole. Drop your half of the Xinhua code phrase and if they know the rest, well? That would mean somethin', wouldn't it?"

"Lemme ask you: Where is true west?"

"Depends where you're standing," you respond.

"Nope. Where is true west?" he asks again.

You hesitate to answer.

"Personally, I'd say to follow the evening redness. But that's just me," Wayne says, and gives you a wink.

"So, the dead drop," Wayne continues. "You know the embassy on this station? There's a ship and home kiosks next door with a planter in the corner. Ficus or some shit. If you really want to show loyalty to God's Great GalCon, rummage around in there, sneaky beaky like. Had to move that thing like ten times last month and honestly I'm gettin' a little tired of it."

Wayne leans back, tips his cap and holds up two more fingers. "Shot for the road?"

He drains the little cup like he's done it a million times before. You eye your own drink with obvious suspicion, given the circumstances. 

"More for me then, I guess," he says, and drinks your glass down before sauntering out of the bar without paying.
strSetPlotObjective: name|Proxy War: Prove Your Loyalty|ct|TIsProspectorBCER|desc|Prove your worth with Titan. Maybe Pan Tao can help?

strDesc:
Pan Tao rolls his eyes at your approach, then lights a new cigarette using his first. "How'd that go?" he asks without looking at you.

"About as well as you'd expect," you reply.

Pan Tao frowns and nods. "Yeah," he says. "Wayne loves his little 'aw-shucks' hayseed act. Don't let it fool you. Guy probably has eyes on us right now."  

Less attitude than before, at least. Helpful, even.

"If there even is one," Pan says. "Rumors, hearsay. Every drunk on this rock has a story. I've damn near lost track."

"Tell me one," you say.

"Well. Couple days ago an atmo system near residential hit the fritz, right? Not so abnormal at first. The station is a shithole. But then, all the way across the rock, another one went down. Then another. You see where this is going."

"Not a coincidence," you reply.

"Could be! That's the rub. Look, if there's really a Xinhua rat this deep in our network, they'd be smart. Very smart. A skilled enough hacker to do that and more. They'd know how to talk, too. Good with oligarchs, good with the military brass. A real 'friend to all' type. Otherwise, how would they get access to intel?"

Useful. "Any other advice?" you ask.

"Shit," he says. "We didn't even have this conversation."
"A fellow painter I see," Pan says. "I'll tell you what I tell everyone: start with the exit plan. Things always go down faster than you think. Once the deed is done, I mean."
"Not my area," Pan says. "I'm more of a hands-on kinda guy."

"Sorry, can we run this back?" you say. Something is bothering you. Something niggling at the edge of memory and time.

"Mm? To what, or where, my friend?" She smiles.

"It was something you said before," you say. She's playing with her necklace again. The glassy pearls sliding along the string, clinking softly as they rub against their mates.

What was it she said? Something about Calico City. "I'm sorry," you say, blinking. "It's not coming to me, whatever it is."

"That's perfectly alright."

"Have we met before?" you ask her suddenly. You don't think you have - it's a sensation, an impression, rather than a recollection. Perhaps you've met her sister. "Have you ever been to K-Leg?"

"Oh, certainly not," she says. "I've been there once or twice, but I would remember if we had crossed paths."

"That makes sense," you say. "Yeah. Forget I asked."

Your encounter with Eleni ends there, on that note, with only the customary sorting of payment and debt to plow through - a neutral and empty space, in contrast to the strangeness of the whole sit-down. She insists on paying. You let her, and promise to get the next one, which is never going to happen.

You amble back to the concourse to bid your final goodbyes. The desperation of the shoppers and the sellers seems muted now, and no more greeters try to inveigle you into their stores, such is the change in your aura.

"Be seeing you," Eleni says. She makes a curious circle gesture with one hand - a goodbye? - and is gone.

What an odd duck.

"Scratch that," you say, "don't forget I asked. I want to nail this down, whatever it is."

"Mm?" she says, smiling politely, meaninglessly.

That's it. That's what it is.

"You said," you say slowly. It's as if you're on the cusp of waking. The words are there, but struggling to be said. "You said the Calicoans ..."

"Yes," she says unhappily.

"You said they were taught to worship a way of life that never was ..."

"I did," she says. "I did say that." She scowls. But it's just an expression. There's no feeling behind it.

"A man on K-Leg said something very similar to me before I left," you say.

She waves a hand questioningly.

"I'm going to ask again," you say. "Tell me the truth. Do I know you?"

Eleni stops fidgeting with her necklace, and places her hands in her lap. "Well, now. That's one question I can't help you with."

Her eyes, behind her thick glasses, are magnified like a bug's. The overblown pupils reach the hard edges of the frame as they dart around, scanning the room. They recentre, and she fixes you with a strangely steely gaze.

Inside that steel, a trace of gold.

The name comes unbidden to your lips, and once arrived, refuses to leave. It doesn't make sense, and yet out it comes. "... Smiley?"

The question hangs between you like a smart munition searching for a target.

She smiles at you. No more maternal beneficence. It recalls Smiley's fixed, dopey trademark - but with a new element, a wildcard that turns the wide silly expression predatory.

"It's me. In the flesh," she - they? He? - says, and sighs. "The flesh and like a kilo of silicone prosthetics, anyway. Shit. [us-firstname], how've you been?"

"How have I been?" you say hollowly. "Fuck you. Whoever you are, go fuck yourself. What is going on?"

"I'm trying to help you," she says - you settle on she for now, with nothing else to go on. "You wandered away from K-LEG and wound up at Ceres, from the frying pan into the fire, truly. And I suppose I have a soft spot for a fellow AV Clubber."

"I want nothing more to do with you." You stand up. Heads turn your way. You're not bothering to lower your voice.

"Sit down," she says levelly. One of her hands, under the table, seems to be tracking your every movement. 

You ease back into your chair. You've seen people in similar situations, in crowded rooms on K-LEG. You try desperately to remember how they ended.

"Thank you," she says conversationally, as if you had passed her a sauce packet. She runs a tongue along her teeth, then reaches into her mouth. She spits into her hand, and tosses a large set of dentures onto the table. The long white teeth drip, saliva strung between the points.

"That," she says, again running a tongue around her mouth, "was driving me crazy."

"What happens now?" you ask. "We're just talking," she says. It's surreal: Smiley and Eleni, the thesis and the antithesis, swim together, pooling into something new. "Talking normally, calmly. Let's not put Niko out. I had to learn Greek for this bit, I don't want to burn it." "So you're not Greek." "I am not." "Then what?" "An Episcopalian." She shrugs. "What's it to you?" "You got all your 'friends' on K-Leg killed, or shipped off to Prokofiev," you hiss. "I barely got out. That's what it is to me." "That," she says, appearing a little hurt, "was not my fault. That was quite a setback for me, actually. I'm picking up the pieces." "You think you're a victim in all this?" "I didn't say that," she says, smiling hungrily. "It's that old adage - you know, 'nobody thinks of themselves as a villain'. Right? When an adult says it to a child, they're implying: 'therefore, because it's relative, there's no such thing as a villain!' An early pitfall in your conception of other people, and people shoot right on through to adulthood without revisiting it." You stare across at the table. "What the fuck are you talking about?" "I'm trying to say, a single counterexample torpedoes the whole thing." She points to herself. "And that's me. I'm the counterexample." You don't want to repeat yourself, so you think of the next most pertinent question. "Can I go now?" Smiley, Eleni, whoever she is, edges out of the booth first. "Way ahead of you. It's on my tab." You can see the pistol now. At least you weren't falling for a bluff - that's nice to know. She stows it under her coat. "I really was trying to help," she says. "Be seeing you." She slips out of the cafe. The host looks up at her departure, frowning. You finish your coffee, trying to shake a sudden attack of depersonalisation. The videotape ... not for the first time since K-Leg, you wish you'd never found it.
